title.full: Canadian Energy Outlook, 3rd edition – Pathways for a net-zero Canada: Horizon 2060

publisher.full: Institut de l'énergie Trottier, Polytechnique Montréal

description: Exploratory Canadian reference: in-force plus proposed federal rules (CER, ZEV mandate); no GHG cap.
pathwayDescription: Published in 2024 by the Institut de l’énergie Trottier (Polytechnique Montréal) as part of the third Canadian Energy Outlook, Pathways for a net-zero Canada – Horizon 2060, the study explores, province by province, the least-cost pathways for transforming Canada’s energy system and reaching net-zero emissions. The Reference scenario (REF) is an exploratory pathway that projects Canada’s energy system to 2060. It includes the policies in force in 2024, plus two federal measures that were still drafts at the time: the Clean Electricity Regulations and the Zero-Emission Vehicle sales mandate. It sets no emissions target. Emissions fall about 14% below 2005 levels by 2030 and about 25% by 2050, far short of Canada’s 2030 target and its net-zero goal. Light-duty transport electrifies almost completely. Energy production, dominated by crude oil, keeps growing until 2050, and buildings, industry and heavy transport change only slowly.

coreDrivers.policies: Carbon price rise to $170/t CO2e in 2030, then is indexed to inflation. Draft Clean Electricity Regulations version from November 2023 is included and pushes gas and coal out of power. Clean Fuel Regulations double transport biofuel use by 2030. ZEV sales represnets 60% in 2030, and 100% in 2035, electrifies 95.4% of road passenger demand by 2050. Investment Tax Credits supports Clean-technology, hydrogen and CCUS expandion and ZEV incentives.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: North American TIMES Energy Model minimises total energy-system cost to 2060, so technology unit costs decide build-out within the policy constraints. Falling costs drive electrification beyond the mandates: hydrogen trucks penetrate after 2040 'as costs decrease', and more cost-effective generation pushes electricity demand to ~3,000 PJ by 2050 even without a GHG cap. Gas keeps a large share of industry and buildings because it remains cheapest absent a constraint.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: GDP and population growth (Statistics Canada medium-growth) drive service demand; REF uses CER Current Policies export prices, keeping crude oil production ~18% above 2021 through 2050. As the pathway without an emissions constraint, these macro and export-price assumptions are its dominant driver alongside existing policy.

dependencies.dependency_description: Power decarbonisation in REF rests mainly on the August 2023 draft Clean Electricity Regulations (approved in December 2024) and carbon pricing, which cut power emissions from 77 to 4.6 Mt by 2050, while the ZEV mandate and building electrification raise demand to ~2,977 PJ. Coal retirement timing differs by province. If the draft CER is weakened or delayed, this trajectory loses its main lever; no supporting strategy for storage or grids is modelled.

Utilities and regulators vary widely in their readiness to approve anticipatory investment and smart two-way grids, and investment barriers push Canadian infrastructure costs above Europe’s. These frameworks set how quickly REF’s grid upgrades can be approved and financed. The supply is already near limit as Hydro-Québec already refuses full heating electrification for lack of peak capacity.

Renewables are the cheapest generation today and in the medium term, but keeping the existing nuclear fleet past the 2040s needs costly investment, and SMR costs stay unconfirmed until a first unit runs. Investment in the electricity sector is named as an implementation challenge; the companion analysis finds electrification brings system savings that are unevenly shared, so tariff design matters.

REF adds only 4.6 GW of SMRs by 2050 and modest wind growth, so social acceptance of new nuclear or large projects is a limited constraint; the report flags social acceptance as a general implementation barrier and SMR acceptance as uncertain. This may also vary per region, as some region already committed to SMR deployment.

Power demand growth follows mandated EV uptake and heat-pump adoption; electrified heating shifts the peak to winter, and demand-shifting strategies would reduce required capacity. REF's lower heating electrification keeps this dependency smaller than in net-zero pathways.

REF still needs large grid and storage expansion - storage reaches 14.3 GW (6.3 GW centralized batteries, 5.3 GW pumped hydro) and generation grows 28% - with winter-peak capacity built ahead of demand. The model uses a cost premium for grid ancillary costs and no hourly dispatch, so curtailment and storage needs are only approximated. The supply is already near limit as Hydro-Québec already refuses full heating electrification for lack of peak capacity.

REF relies on not-yet-commercial SMRs (0.5 GW in 2030, 4.6 GW in 2050) and grid-scale batteries (6.3 GW by 2050). SMRs 'have yet to reach commercial scale anywhere'; delays would shift REF toward more gas or wind. Low-cost long-duration storage (e.g. iron-air) could reshape the mix but is not assumed.
Grid build-out faces supply-chain constraints for generation, transmission and distribution components, but REF's moderate growth and limited biomass use keep resource limits non-binding.
not applicable.

Expanding generation and grids competes for workers with building retrofits and heat-pump installation; the report warns of labour shortages, and Hydro-Québec's plan alone needs ~35,000 construction workers (11% of Quebec's). REF's slower build-out keeps this below the net-zero pathways.

REF's 34% steel emission cut by 2050 (13.6 to 9.0 Mt) rests largely on one modelled policy - Ontario and federal funding to phase out coal use at Algoma and ArcelorMittal Dofasco - which electrifies Ontario steel and cuts subsector energy use 42% by 2030. Beyond this, only carbon pricing and the OBPS apply; no national steel strategy is modelled.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: National power-generation emissions in MtCO2e, Scope 1, including negative emissions from BECCS power. Fuel extraction for power sits in 'Oil, gas and coal production' and is not separable. 2021 baseline differs slightly across Explorer scenario files (75.1-77.1 Mt)

granularity: High-carbon assets lifetime face early retirement policy
byMetric.scopeLimitations: Retirement is regulation-driven via the CER, which excludes Nunavut, Northwest Territories, Yukon and remote communities; existing units are modelled individually. No asset-lifetime table is published.

Installed capacity, GW. Storage figure covers centralized batteries, decentralized batteries, pumped hydro, flywheel and hydrogen storage; one combined series in the report figure, broken down by type in the Explorer export - 2050 total 14.3 GW (6.3 centralized battery, 2.7 decentralized battery, 5.3 pumped hydro). Decentralized (rooftop) PV and batteries reported separately in Explorer. No captive industrial series.

Derived: 'Electricity production' emissions ('Figure 4.8') / generation excl. storage ('Figure 2.5'). Scope 1 CO2e. BECCS power is netted in, so intensity is negative in net-zero pathways by 2050. Explorer 'Electricity' emissions also include a 'Heat' line, excluded here. Distributed (rooftop) PV included in generation.

Electricity generation in PJ. Figure lists a small 'Storage' output line (1-35 PJ), excluded here. Explorer separates centralized and decentralized (rooftop) PV. On-grid and distributed generation are both included; no captive industrial series. Provincial generation by source exists for all 13 jurisdictions in the Chapter 5 dataset.

LIMITATION - period totals: values are 10-year period totals, each covering the decade ending in its label year (2040 = 2031-2040); divide by 10 for an annual average (e.g. NZ50 2041-2050 $509bn -> ~$51bn/yr). Reviewer interpretation, not documented in the export; discounting basis unknown. Aggregate electricity-sector investment in $ (Power10=3), plus 'Fix operation cost'. No technology split, no 2021 value.

Investment cost for 2022, 2030, 2050 and one fixed O&M value per technology; no variable O&M or fuel costs shown. Two SMR rows: optimistic (REF, NZ50) and pessimistic (NZ50PS). Storage split into 4h/8h utility batteries, decentralized batteries, pumped hydro and compressed air (peak and seasonal). No transmission costs.
Derived: technology generation / total generation excl. storage. Not reported directly as shares. Provincial generation technology mix also exists for all 13 jurisdictions in the Chapter 5 dataset.

Iron and steel = combustion ('Figure 4.6') + process ('Figure 4.7') emissions, MtCO2e, Scope 1. Ironmaking and steelmaking not separated; no power-related (Scope 2) emissions; any steel CCS is not attributed (industrial CCS reported only economy-wide, 'Figure 4.9').
Only two steel options are costed: hydrogen direct iron reduction and CCS capture (as a capex multiplier); no costs for conventional BF-BOF, EAF or scrap routes. Values constant 2022-2050.
